THOUSANDS OF YEARS
If reaching Type One
is difficult, stepping
up to Type Two
borders on the divine.
A Type Two civilization
needs billions of times
more power than reaches
a single planet.
What kind of engineering
would it take to
swallow the light of a star?
Physicist Freeman Dyson
suggested that such a
civilization might build
a vast swarm of
solar collectors completely
surrounding a sun.
Such a megastructure,
known as a Dyson
sphere, would give a
civilization a staggering
amount of power,
though no one has
ever found one.
Beyond a single solar
system lies the
incomprehensible expanse
of the galactic spiral.
A Type Three civilization
would not stop at
one sun; it would
harvest hundreds of billions
of stars across a
galaxy about a hundred
thousand light-years wide.
Some theoretical models
suggest such a society
might even extract
rotational energy from
supermassive black holes.
Traveling between star
systems might be as
routine to them as
taking a morning train
is to you.
To a society operating
at this galactic scale,
our entire recorded history
would look like a
momentary spark.
Dyson's idea is easy
to misunderstand.
It is not a
single solid shell wrapped
around a star.
The proposal is a
vast swarm of solar
collectors, each catching
a share of the
light, together surrounding
the sun.
A star pours out
light in every direction,
and almost all of
it travels off into
empty space.
A civilization that captured
it would be turning
a wasteful stream of
light into a source of power.
Be clear, though,
about what is theory.
No one has seen
a Type Three civilization,
and no one knows
if one exists.
A Type Three civilization
would command a whole galaxy.
To such a society,
our recorded history would
be a momentary spark.
We measure our history
in thousands of years.
It is a humbling
thought, and it reminds
us how young our
civilization is.
The idea that such
a society might draw
rotational energy from
supermassive black holes
comes from theoretical
models, not observation.
Treat it as a
way of stretching the
imagination to the limit
of what physics allows.
